title: Matching Engines and Price-Time Priority
objectives: State the price-time priority rule and apply it to a queue of orders
Step through a sequence of incoming orders and determine every trade, price and remaining book state
Explain why the resting order's price wins in a cross
Describe queue position and why microseconds of arrival order have economic value
motivation: When a buy at \$100.02 meets a sell at \$99.99, which price executes? The answer is decided by the matching engine's priority rules, and those rules shape how every participant trades, from why market makers race to update quotes to why your order sometimes fills at a better price than you offered. Walking a matching engine by hand is the fastest way to internalise market behaviour.

items: **Price priority**: better prices first. Bids: highest buys first. Asks: lowest sells first.
**Time priority**: at equal price, the order that arrived earlier fills first, first in, first out (FIFO) within each price level.
**Crossing rule**: when a new marketable order meets a resting order, the trade executes at the **resting order's price**, the reward for having supplied liquidity first.

blocks.md: These three rules, price, then time, then resting-price execution, are the heart of price-time priority matching, used by most major exchanges (some venues add pro-rata or size priority for particular products, but the logic here generalises). An order that cannot immediately trade *rests* in the book; one that can is a *marketable limit order*, aggressive even though it is technically a limit order.

blocks.text: Walking the engine: seven orders, step by step

blocks.md: A matching engine is a deterministic function from an incoming order and a book state to a new book state plus zero or more fills. That sounds bureaucratic until you realise that *everything* about market fairness, who gets filled, at what price, in what order, is decided by two tie-break rules the engine applies: price priority first, then time priority within a price. There is no judgement call inside the engine. That is the point.

blocks.title: Worked match: a market buy arrives at a resting book
items: An aggressive **market buy for 600** arrives. Price priority scans ask levels upward: everything at $100.10$ is cheaper than anything at $100.12$.
At $100.10$ two orders rest. Time priority ranks them by arrival: the $300$ from 09:30:01 is first, then the $500$ from 09:30:04.
Fills: $300@100.10$ (fully filled, removed), $300@100.10$ against the second order (partially filled, $200$ remains resting at $100.10$). The incoming order is fully satisfied and disappears.
Post-trade book state: asks are now $200@100.10$, $400@100.12$, $200@100.15$. Note the $100.12$ order arrived *earlier* than the $100.15$ one but sits at a better price, price always outranks time.

blocks.md: Two consequences follow. First, **queue position is an asset**: an order resting at a popular price is effectively holding an option on being filled, and strategies that cancel-and-replace pay for it with queue loss. Second, the engine's determinism is what makes a provable audit trail possible, given the same sequence of inputs, any correct re-implementation produces the same fills, which is how exchanges defend themselves in disputes.

blocks.title: Where you will meet this
blocks.md: Interview favourite: *"You are first in queue at the best bid; a market sell for 10× your size arrives, what happens to your fill?"* Answer: you are filled fully at your price before anyone behind you gets anything. Follow-up: what if the incoming order was priced *through* the book? Then it sweeps levels, each level fills in time order until the incoming price limit binds.

rows: Later designs (e.g. pro-rata in some futures) change queueing strategy fundamentally
Price improvement exists in some venues; matters for expected fill quality
A firm's own two orders must not wash volume
Odd lots can match after round lots on some venues

blocks.title: Hypothetical sequence on one symbol (all quantities in shares)
items: **1. Buy limit 500 @ 100.00.** Empty book: no match; it rests. Book: bid 500@100.00.
**3. Buy limit 200 @ 100.02.** Crosses the resting ask. Trade: **200 @ 100.02** (resting price). Remaining: ask 100@100.02. The buyer's aggressive limit just paid the full spread.
**4. Sell limit 400 @ 99.99.** 99.99 < best bid 100.00, crosses. Trade: **400 @ 100.00** (resting bid's price). Remaining: bid 100@100.00.
**5. Buy limit 300 @ 100.01.** Best ask is 100.02; 100.01 does not reach it. Rests. Book: bids 300@100.01 and 100@100.00; ask 100@100.02.
**6. Buy limit 200 @ 100.01.** Same price as step 5's bid, joins the back of the FIFO queue. Bids: 300@100.01 (older), 200@100.01 (newer), 100@100.00.

**7. Sell limit 250 @ 100.01.** Crosses the 100.01 bid level. Time priority: the older 300-lot fills first. Trade: **250 @ 100.01**; the remaining bid queue is 50@100.01 (old) ahead of 200@100.01 (new).

blocks.caption: Replay the worked sequence: watch trades print at the resting order's price and the queue form behind equal-priced bids.

blocks.text: Why queue position is a traded asset

blocks.md: Step 7 shows the economics: of 250 shares sold, all went to the *older* 300-lot. Being first in the FIFO queue converts directly into fill probability, so firms invest in the fastest links to the exchange, colocation, direct feeds, kernel-bypass networking, to gain microseconds of arrival-time advantage. Note what matters is the *engine's* receipt order, not your send order: two packets arriving nearly simultaneously are sequenced by the venue, which is why latency competition exists at all.

blocks.title: Matching engines are deterministic
blocks.md: Given the same sequence of order events, a price-time engine produces exactly the same trades, no randomness anywhere. This determinism is what makes exchange simulators faithful: you can unit-test your strategy logic against a replayed book and get identical fills to a recorded session (modulo data completeness).

blocks.title: Partial fills and resting remainder
blocks.md: Every match consumes only the smaller of the two quantities; the larger order survives with the remainder. Step 3 traded 200 of a 300-lot sell, the remaining 100 stayed at the front of its queue. Forgetting the remainder is the classic bug in hand-rolled matching engines.

guidedExercise.prompt: Continue the sequence: step 8 is a **sell limit 150 @ 100.00**. State which order(s) it trades with, at what price(s), the trade quantity, and the resulting bid-side book (prices and queue order).
hints: A sell at 100.00 crosses the best bid 100.01, not 100.00.
Time priority inside the 100.01 level: the 50-share remainder is older than the 200-share order.
guidedExercise.solution: The sell crosses bids at 100.01. Trade: **150 @ 100.01**, taken entirely from the older 50@100.01 first, then 100 more from the 200@100.01 order. After: 50@100.01 (fully filled, removed) and 100@100.01 remaining, then 100@100.00 behind it. The resting-price rule paid the resting bids their quoted 100.01.

independentExercise.prompt: Starting from an empty book: (1) sell limit 600 @ 10.05 rests; (2) buy limit 250 @ 10.07 arrives; (3) buy limit 100 @ 10.05 arrives; (4) sell limit 200 @ 10.05 arrives. For each step, give any trade (quantity and price) and the book state. What is the ask-side queue at the end, and why does step 4 produce no trade?
hints: Step 3: decide whether a buy priced exactly at the best ask is marketable (it is: buy price $\ge$ best ask).
Step 4: a sell crosses only against *bids*, check whether any bids exist by then.
independentExercise.solution: Step 1: no trade; ask 600@10.05. Step 2: the buy crosses the resting ask, trade **250 @ 10.05** (resting ask's price); ask remainder 350@10.05. Step 3: a buy at 10.05 with best ask 10.05 crosses, because a buy price $\ge$ best ask is marketable, trade **100 @ 10.05**; ask remainder 250@10.05. Step 4: the sell at 10.05 looks for bids to cross, none exist, so it rests on the ask side *behind* the older 250@10.05 (time priority). No trade occurs because no bid exists to cross.

commonMistakes: Executing crosses at the incoming order's price instead of the resting order's price, the resting side earned its price by waiting.
Ignoring the FIFO queue at a price level: equal-price orders fill oldest first.
Forgetting the unfilled remainder of the larger order stays in the book.
Believing a buy at exactly the ask cannot cross, buy price $\ge$ best ask matches in standard engines.
realWorldApplication: Exchange matching engines (NYSE, Nasdaq, CME, crypto venues) implement these rules in low-latency software; compliance teams reconstruct the exact book from order-level audit trails to investigate trade executions, using precisely the step-by-step replay shown here.
quantFinanceApplication: Backtesters and execution simulators implement price-time matching to generate fills; a quant dev who can walk this algorithm by hand can audit the simulator that decides whether a strategy looks profitable.
summary: Priority is price first, then time (FIFO within a price level), and crosses execute at the resting order's price.
Marketable limit orders cross the spread immediately; non-marketable ones rest and provide liquidity.
Partial fills leave the remainder resting, keeping its queue priority.
Queue position has economic value, which is why latency competition exists, the engine's arrival order decides fills.

quiz.prompt: A new buy limit at 100.02 meets a resting sell at 100.00. At what price does the trade execute?
quiz.explanation: The resting order's price wins: it supplied liquidity first, and the aggressor accepts that price to trade immediately.

quiz.prompt: Two buy orders rest at the same price. Which fills first when a sell arrives?
options: The one from the faster broker
quiz.explanation: Price-time priority uses time as the tie-breaker at equal price: first in, first out. (Some derivatives venues use pro-rata, but the standard equity rule is FIFO.)

quiz.prompt: Book: ask 100@100.02. An incoming buy limit for 200 @ 100.02 executes fully. How many shares remain at the 100.02 ask level?
quiz.explanation: The resting 100 shares fill; the level is exhausted and removed, the incoming order's remainder (100 shares) would then rest as a new bid at 100.02.

quiz.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why firms pay for colocation and low-latency links in a price-time market.
quiz.modelAnswer: Fill priority within a price level depends on the engine's arrival order, so arriving microseconds earlier converts directly into higher fill probability and better queue position; colocation and fast links buy that arrival advantage.
quiz.explanation: Time priority makes arrival order economically valuable; latency is the mechanism that improves it.

quiz.prompt: A buy limit for 300 @ 99.99 arrives with best ask at 99.98. What happens?
options: No trade, the buy price is above the ask, which is illegal
It rests as a bid at 99.99
quiz.explanation: Buy $\ge$ best ask means marketable: it fills immediately at the resting ask's 99.98. If a remainder existed it would rest at 99.99 as the new best bid.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about matching engines are TRUE?
options: They are deterministic: same event sequence, same trades
Partial fills leave the unfilled remainder resting with its original priority
They always execute at the mid-price
quiz.explanation: Engines are deterministic replays of their event streams, remainders keep their queue position, and price priority is evaluated before time priority. Mid-price execution is not part of standard price-time matching.

flashcards.back: Price priority first (best prices), then FIFO within each price level; crosses execute at the resting order's price.

flashcards.front: Whose price wins in a cross?
flashcards.back: The resting (liquidity-providing) order's price, the aggressor pays the quoted price to trade immediately.
A limit order whose price crosses the opposite best quote; it executes immediately like a market order but with a price cap/floor.
FIFO means earlier arrival fills first when liquidity trades at that level, so arrival time maps directly to fill probability.
